title: CS102_Unit1e_Unit_1e_-_Extras
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 1e, described as 'good-to-know' extra material intended for self-study and exploration rather than core required content.
main_text: Unit 1e - Extras. 'Good-to-know' Extra Material for Self-Study/Exploration.
notes_text: This unit is framed as supplementary/enrichment content, distinct from the core curriculum covered in earlier units.

title: CS102_Unit1e_Extra_Topics
summary: Lists the six supplementary topics covered in this unit, ranging from C++ namespace conventions to I/O manipulators, char/ASCII handling, input error behavior, and random numbers.
main_text:
Extra Topics:
- Why "using namespace std;"
- Why endl if we have '\n'?
- Other I/O Manipulators
- Understanding chars, ASCII, integers, and arithmetic
- Bad input to cin
- Random numbers

title: CS102_Unit1e_More_cin_and_cout
summary: Section divider slide introducing the next group of topics: deeper coverage of cin and cout behavior.
notes_text: This is a section-header slide marking the transition into I/O-stream-focused topics (cin, cout, streams, manipulators).

title: CS102_Unit1e_I_O_Streams
summary: Explains that C++ and the OS use buffered streams to move data, with cin extracting from stdin and cout inserting into stdout, illustrated with keyboard-to-memory and memory-to-screen diagrams.
notes_text: The diagrams show data flowing from a physical keyboard through the OS into an 'input stream memory (stdin)' that cin reads from, and separately from a program's cout calls through the OS into an 'output stream memory (stdout)' that is ultimately displayed on a monitor.

images.description: A diagram showing a physical keyboard sending keystrokes down through the OS into a row of memory cells labeled 'input stream memory (stdin)', which cin then extracts from into a program's int variable, illustrated alongside the corresponding C++ code.

A diagram showing a C++ program's cout statements flowing into a row of memory cells labeled 'output stream memory (stdout)', which the OS then copies to a monitor screen displaying 'It was the', illustrating how cout output is buffered before being shown.

title: CS102_Unit1e_std_and_the_using_namespace_statement
summary: Explains that most C++ library components live in the std namespace (analogous to folders), so cout and endl are technically std::cout and std::endl, and that 'using namespace std;' lets the compiler find them without the std:: prefix.

images.description: A folder-hierarchy diagram showing the root directory branching to a 'std' folder, which contains three items labeled cout, endl, and cin, visually representing the std namespace as a classification hierarchy similar to a filesystem.

title: CS102_Unit1e_Error_without_using_statement
summary: Shows a terminal/editor screenshot demonstrating the compiler error that results from using 'cout' without either the std:: prefix or a 'using namespace std;' statement.
main_text: Error without 'using' statement. A screenshot shows the source file lec02-cout.cpp with the 'using namespace std;' line commented out, and a line 'cout << "Hello world" << endl;' inside main(). Compiling with g++ produces the error: 'cout' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'std::cout'? The compiler suggests the fix of prefixing with std::.
notes_text: This is a live demonstration referenced in the prior slide, reinforcing that omitting both std:: and the using directive causes a compile-time 'not declared in this scope' error, with the compiler itself suggesting std::cout as the fix.

images.description: A terminal and code editor screenshot showing a C++ source file (lec02-cout.cpp) with the 'using namespace std;' line commented out and an unqualified 'cout' call, followed by a g++ compilation error stating that 'cout' was not declared in this scope and suggesting 'std::cout' instead.
labels: error: 'cout' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'std::cout'?

title: CS102_Unit1e_Newlines_endl_and_Flushing
summary: Introduces the '\n' character for moving to a new line and explains that cout only hands characters to the OS, which may delay printing; endl combines '\n' with a forced flush of the output stream.
main_text:
To move the cursor to the next line we need to print a new line, '\n' (char). cout only gives the characters to the OS, which then copies them to the screen. The OS may choose to delay and not print immediately, causing strange issues. endl = '\n' + a flush of the output stream, which forces the OS to print immediately.

Example without flush: cout << "Hi\n"; -- the OS may delay printing ('maybe I'll do it now, maybe later').
Example with flush: cout << "Hi" << endl; -- the OS prints immediately ('your wish is my command').
notes_text: The comic-style illustration personifies cout and the OS in a dialogue: without endl, the OS may procrastinate on printing; with endl, the OS complies immediately.

images.description: A two-panel comic-style illustration personifying cout as a frog asking the OS to print text. In the top panel, cout uses '\n' and the OS replies dismissively that it may delay printing. In the bottom panel, cout uses endl (explicitly mentioning 'flushing') and the OS immediately complies, printing 'Hi' to the screen right away.
labels: Pshh! I'm busy. Maybe I'll do it now, maybe later.

title: CS102_Unit1e_Newlines_endl_and_Flushing_Debugging_Example
summary: Extends the endl/flushing explanation with a debugging example showing that using '\n' can hide a crash's location in output, while endl (which flushes) reveals exactly which line executed before a segmentation fault.
notes_text: This is the practical payoff of the endl-vs-'\n' distinction: unflushed '\n' output can be lost when a program crashes, hiding useful debugging information, whereas endl's forced flush guarantees prior output is visible before a crash.

images.description: Side-by-side code and terminal output comparison: the left panel uses '\n' and shows only '<Segmentation fault>' with no prior output visible, while the right panel uses endl and shows 'Got Here 1' printed before the '<Segmentation fault>', demonstrating how flushing preserves debugging output before a crash.
labels: Use descriptive messages and endls when debugging.

title: CS102_Unit1e_I_O_Manipulators
summary: Introduces I/O manipulators (setw, setprecision, fixed, boolalpha) that control how cout formats output and how cin interprets input, requiring the <iomanip> header, with a worked example of setprecision and fixed.
notes_text: See also: http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/io/manip and the 'iomanip' in-class exercise for exploring various manipulator options.

title: CS102_Unit1e_Understanding_ASCII_and_chars
summary: Explains that a char is a 1-byte integer type where cout's interpretation (character vs. number) depends on the variable's declared type, and shows how ASCII arithmetic works, alongside a reference ASCII printable character table.
notes_text: The variable trace shows: char c holds 97 (displayed as 'a'), char d holds 98 (displayed as 'b'), and int x holds 97 then 49, depending on whether it's assigned from a char or a char literal like '1'.

images.description: A reference table of ASCII printable characters listing decimal codes 32-126 alongside their corresponding characters (space, punctuation, digits, uppercase and lowercase letters), used to look up the numeric value behind any printable character.

title: CS102_Unit1e_Unexpected_Inputs
summary: Explains that cin's '>>' operator stops at unexpected non-whitespace characters without discarding them, leaving variables unchanged and causing subsequent reads to fail too, illustrated with a rectangle/triangle area program given malformed input.
notes_text: This demonstrates a key failure mode of cin: leading non-numeric characters cause silent failure with garbage/uninitialized variable values rather than a runtime crash.

images.description: A diagram showing a confused character extracting data from an input stream containing 'x y 1.25 2 ...'; cin attempts to read into double variables b and h but both remain marked '??' (undefined) because the leading non-numeric characters halted extraction before any valid number was read.

title: CS102_Unit1e_cin_Question
summary: Poses and answers what happens when a double is typed where an integer is expected, or numeric digits are typed where a string is expected, tracing how cin partially consumes tokens across mismatched types.
notes_text: This illustrates that cin>>int stops consuming at the first non-integer character (like '.'), leaving the rest of the token in the stream to be picked up by the next extraction, which can shift values unexpectedly across subsequent variables.

images.description: A step-by-step diagram tracing how cin consumes the raw input stream '1.5 42\n103.25\n' across four extraction operations: first pulling only '1' into int x (leaving '.5' behind), then '.5' into double y, then '42' into double z, and finally '103.25' into a string s, showing how partial-token consumption cascades through multiple variables.

title: CS102_Unit1e_Randomness
summary: Section divider slide introducing the topic of random number generation in C++.
notes_text: This is a section-header slide marking the transition to coverage of pseudo-random number generation using rand(), RAND_MAX, and srand().

title: CS102_Unit1e_Random_Number_Generator
summary: Presents a minimal C++ program demonstrating the rand() function and RAND_MAX constant from <cstdlib>, including commented-out srand() seeding calls.
notes_text: The commented-out srand() calls hint at the upcoming discussion of seeding; without calling srand(), rand() uses a default seed and produces the same sequence on every run.

title: CS102_Unit1e_rand_and_RAND_MAX
summary: Explains that rand() from <cstdlib> returns a pseudo-random integer between 0 and RAND_MAX, and demonstrates how to derive a simulated coin flip and a uniform random fraction between 0 and 1 from it.
notes_text: The number line diagram shows the full range of rand()'s possible output from 0 to RAND_MAX, visually motivating why comparing against RAND_MAX/2 produces a roughly 50/50 split for a coin-flip simulation.

images.description: A number line spanning from 0 to RAND_MAX, representing the full range of possible integer values returned by rand(), used to illustrate how the range can be split (e.g., at the midpoint) or scaled to derive other kinds of random outcomes.

title: CS102_Unit1e_Seeding_Random_Number_Generator
summary: Explains that rand() produces the same sequence on every program run unless seeded differently, and shows how srand(time(0)) seeds the RNG with the current time so each execution produces a different sequence, with a caution to call srand() only once.
main_text:
Re-running a program that calls rand() will generate the same sequence of random numbers (each run will be exactly the same). If we want each execution of the program to be different, we need to seed the RNG with a different value.

srand(int seed) is a function in <cstdlib> to seed the RNG with the value of seed. Unless seed changes from execution to execution, we'll still have the same problem.

Solution: Seed it with the day and time [returned by the time() function defined in ctime]:
srand( time(0) ); // only do this once at the start of the program
int r = rand(); // now call rand() as many times as you want
int r2 = rand(); // another random number
// sequence of random #'s will be different for each execution of program

Important: Only call srand() ONCE at the start of the program, not each time you want to call rand()!

Approximate rand() function (illustrative internal formula):
val = ((val * 1103515245) + 12345) % RAND_MAX;
notes_text: The closing formula is a simplified illustration of a linear congruential generator, similar to how rand() is often implemented internally, to demystify how deterministic seeding produces a repeatable sequence.
